group: PSI Score: Pneumonia Severity Index for CAP
question:
Patient note:
An 88-year-old man was transferred by wheelchair van from the skilled nursing facility where he has lived for the past three years after staff noticed a two-day progression of fever, productive cough, and new need for supplemental pillows at night; he requested transport before receiving any acetaminophen, nebulized bronchodilators, intravenous fluids, or oxygen so the hospital team could evaluate him “in his natural state.” Facility records list hypertension, diet-controlled type 2 diabetes, and a right middle cerebral artery infarction seven years ago that left him with a subtle left hand clumsiness but full independence in speech and cognition; he follows a local neurologist annually and has not experienced additional cerebrovascular events. There is no charted history of chronic kidney impairment, dialysis, malignancy, cirrhosis, viral hepatitis, alcohol-related liver injury, or cardiac pump dysfunction, and his medication profile is limited to lisinopril 10 mg, low-dose aspirin, and a nightly atorvastatin. He quit smoking more than four decades ago, drinks only at holiday toasts, and has never used illicit drugs. On arrival to the ED he sat bolt upright on the gurney, answering orientation questions accurately and conversing in full sentences, though punctuated by a wet, coarse cough that produced yellow-green sputum into a tissue. Skin was flushed and warm, with brisk capillary refill; no peripheral edema or scleral icterus was observed. Pre-intervention vitals obtained immediately after triage placement recorded an oral temperature of 38.55 °C, an irregularly rapid radial pulse that averaged 138 beats per minute on three-lead telemetry showing sinus tachycardia without ectopy, a right-arm blood pressure of 146/74 mm Hg confirmed by manual sphygmomanometer, respirations counted for a full minute at 28 breaths per minute with moderate use of accessory cervical musculature, and fingertip pulse oximetry of 90 % on ambient air at sea-level altitude. Jugular venous contour was not elevated; heart tones revealed a brisk S1 and S2 without murmurs, rubs, or gallops. Lung examination disclosed diminished breath sounds and stony dull percussion over the right posterior costophrenic recess with scattered inspiratory crackles above that level, while the left lung transmitted vesicular breath sounds throughout. The abdomen was scaphoid and nontender, liver span was normal to percussion, and no asterixis or palmar erythema was evident. Neurologic screen demonstrated equal reactive pupils, intact cranial nerves, fluent speech, and 5/5 motor strength on the right with 4+/5 intrinsic hand strength on the left, unchanged from nursing-facility baseline; his Mini-Cog score earlier in the week had been a perfect five. Finger-stick glucose obtained prior to venipuncture read 143 mg/dL. Venous blood drawn within ten minutes of bay entry—before any saline flushes larger than the 2 mL needed to lock the catheter—returned a sodium concentration of 111 mEq/L, potassium 3.8 mEq/L, chloride 90 mEq/L, bicarbonate 12 mEq/L, blood urea nitrogen 70 mg/dL, and serum creatinine 1.0 mg/dL, representing a markedly elevated urea level in the context of preserved glomerular filtration. A complete blood count revealed leukocytes 14.6 × 10⁹/L with 87 % segmented neutrophils, hematocrit 38 %, hemoglobin 12.6 g/dL, and platelets 245 × 10⁹/L. An arterial sample from the right radial artery, drawn while he remained on room air, demonstrated pH 7.15, PaCO₂ 26 mm Hg, PaO₂ 73 mm Hg, and calculated bicarbonate 8 mEq/L, consistent with a severe metabolic acidosis partially compensated by respiratory alkalosis and accompanied by moderate hypoxemia. Serum lactate returned at 2.8 mmol/L. High-sensitivity troponin I was below the analytic threshold. Portable postero-anterior and lateral chest radiographs obtained fifteen minutes into the encounter—still preceding any antimicrobial, diuretic, or ventilatory support—showed a dense consolidation involving the right lower lobe with air bronchograms and a crescentic fluid level that blunted the corresponding costophrenic angle, confirming a reactive pleural collection; cardiac silhouette and mediastinal contours were unchanged from an imaging study performed the previous year. Electrocardiography displayed sinus tachycardia at 138 bpm with nonspecific ST-T changes but no acute ischemia. Two sets of peripheral blood cultures, a nurse-assisted expectorated sputum sample for Gram stain and culture, urinary antigens for Streptococcus pneumoniae and Legionella, and a multiplex respiratory viral PCR panel were dispatched before any empiric therapy. At the point this narrative is dictated he has received no intravenous fluids, vasopressors, bronchodilators, corticosteroids, antipyretics, or supplemental oxygen beyond minimal saline used to flush the arterial catheter, thereby preserving all vital signs, laboratory values, and imaging findings cited above as reflective of his untreated presentation.

Question: What is the patient's Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI)? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
Apply the Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI) to the untreated presentation:
- Demographics: a man's age in years gives 88 points; nursing-facility residence adds 10. Subtotal: 98.
- Comorbidities: prior cerebral infarction qualifies as cerebrovascular disease (+10). Malignancy, liver disease, heart failure, and chronic renal disease are not documented (0 each). Subtotal: 10.
- Examination: pulse 138/min meets the ≥125 threshold (+10). He is oriented, RR 28 is below 30/min, systolic BP 146 is not below 90 mmHg, and temperature 38.55 °C is neither <35 nor ≥40 °C (0 each). Subtotal: 10.
- Tests: arterial pH 7.15 (<7.35) +30; BUN 70 mg/dL (≥30) +20; sodium 111 mEq/L (<130) +20; pleural effusion on radiograph +10. Glucose 143 mg/dL (<250), hematocrit 38% (not <30%), and room-air oxygenation (PaO₂ 73 mmHg, not <60; saturation 90%, not <90%) add 0 each. Subtotal: 80.
Total = 98 + 10 + 10 + 80 = 198.
Final answer: 198
